title: Usage Reprocessor Operator: windowed backfill & idempotent replay orchestration
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem statement: Our Console usage analytics pipeline has multiple historical gaps and schema-evolution mismatches that prevent reliable cost and latency dashboards. Existing one-off reprocess jobs are brittle, expensive, and not idempotent; they risk double-counting and provide poor observability for partial runs. Goal: build an operator and job orchestration surface that can reliably plan, execute, monitor, and resume windowed backfills and selective replays against the analytics ingestion pipeline with strong idempotency and low operational effort.

Scope and non-goals: Build the orchestration layer and supporting components to run windowed backfills for events originating from Console backend services. This includes a coordinator service, job-state persistence, idempotent transform library, and dashboards/alerts. This work does NOT include wholesale refactors of source instrumentation; it will surface schema issues via reports and guardrails but will not convert all producers.

Success metrics:
- Ability to run multi-day backfills up to 30 days without manual intervention.
- End-to-end reprocess throughput >= 50M events/day in parallelized mode.
- No duplicate events in warehouse (measured by uniqueness on event_id + source + event_version) post-run.
- Mean time to detect and retry failures < 15 minutes.
- Dashboard shows per-window progress and estimated completion time within 5% error.

High-level design:
1) Planner / Controller: a stateless control-plane API that accepts a backfill spec (source, from_ts, to_ts, transform_version, priority, target_table). It splits the range into windows (configurable: time-based and size-based) and creates Job shards.
2) Job State Store: persisted job shard records in console-postgres (jobs table) with status transitions: PENDING -> RUNNING -> SUCCEEDED | FAILED | RETRYING | CANCELLED. Each record stores window_range, planner_version, attempt_count, last_error, output_manifest_uri.
3) Worker execution model: idempotent worker that consumes shard work via pull (kafka topic / sqs or direct DB lease). Worker reads raw events from archival store (S3/GCS) or from eventstream replay API, applies schema-aware transform that embeds event_version and transform_version ribbons, deduplicates using event_id keys, writes atomic shard output to staging (Parquet on S3) and emits completion metadata.
4) Dedup and idempotency: deterministic sort+hashing on event_id + source + event_version before write, and write manifests that include checksum and row_count to validate. Re-running same shard should be a no-op if manifest exists and checksums match.
5) Merge job: after all shards for a backfill complete, a merge step validates manifests, runs quality checks (row counts, sample diffs), and atomically swaps the target partition in warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake/Redshift) or appends with dedupe query.
6) Observability & Guardrails: Grafana dashboards per-backfill, per-shard metrics (processed, duplicates, errors), alerting for long-running shards (> SLA), and automatic dynamic throttling to keep cluster costs within budget.

Compatibility and data sources: Support event read from: (a) cold storage archives (S3 paths partitioned by date), (b) stream re-ingestion via our EventStream replay API, and (c) ad-hoc query pulls for legacy tables. For each source we implement a Source Adapter.

Schema evolution strategy: Each transform must declare an event_version and a compatibility policy: backward-compatible, mapping-shim, or fail-fast. The operator will run a lightweight schema check stage per-shard and either auto-apply shims from the transform library or fail the shard and surface a remediation PR link.

Failure & retry semantics: Shards have exponential backoff with jitter and a cap of 5 attempts. Persistent failures escalate to an Incident queue (Slack #analytics-replay) and create a remediation ticket template. Partial outputs are retained for debug for 30 days and can be reprocessed locally.

Access control and safety: Backfill requests require RBAC scope console:backfill:create and will default to a dry-run mode. Sensitive data redaction passes as part of transform pipeline and KMS encryption applies to manifests.

Operational runbook (summary):
- Submit a backfill spec via controller UI or CLI.
- Controller creates shards and writes to jobs table.
- Workers pick up shards and stream status updates.
- Use dashboard to watch progress; failed shards can be retried or re-scoped.
- Merge step validates and swaps data into production tables.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary): implement controller + simple worker reading from S3, run small-scale backfills on non-prod dataset (2 weeks).
- Phase 2 (scale): add stream re-ingestion adapter, robust dedupe logic, and merge step; run 7-day backfills on production clone (3 weeks).
- Phase 3 (ga): enable RBAC, dashboards, and run 30-day backfills; hunt edge cases and harden retries (2 weeks).

Integration points and artifacts:
- Confluence PRD: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/UD-Analytics+Backfill+Operator (owner: Asha Patel)
- Prototype repo: github.com/redwood-inference/console-replay-proto (branch: eng/20567-operator)
- Example runbook: drive.google.com/drive/folders/console-backfill-runbooks

Estimated cost and infra: Expected S3 egress and compute ~ $2.5k/week during large backfills; recommend using spot GPU-less workers (CPU-only) and scale workers horizontally.

Open design decisions:
- Whether to use Kafka-based lease queue vs. DB-lease for shard distribution (DB-lease chosen initially for simplicity; evaluate move to Kafka in Phase 2).
- Warehouse swap strategy: prefer atomic partition swaps in BigQuery/Redshift over in-place dedupe SQL for speed. We need a small experimental comparison task.
- Whether to integrate with existing eventstream-resynthesis service or maintain a separate adapter.

Dependencies: ["ENG-19731", "ENG-13912", "ENG-18204"],

Notes: This ticket focuses on the operator and core idempotent execution path. Separate tickets will track transform library convergence, UI features, and long-term storage lifecycle.
